question:
Patient note:
A 32-year-old man who works as a civil-aviation safety inspector presented this afternoon to the combined rheumatology–pulmonary clinic for a scheduled comprehensive status update before he embarks on a six-week overseas assignment inspecting regional airports in humid equatorial climates. He strode into the office carrying a rolling suitcase and laptop, greeting staff without shortness of breath, and spoke clearly throughout the hour-long interview. At age eight he was given a diagnosis of perennial, moderate persistent asthma after repeated winter admissions for expiratory wheeze and nocturnal cough; since college he has required no hospitalizations, yet baseline spirometry performed last month revealed an FEV1 of 2.6 L (72 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.66 that improved only 6 % post-albuterol. He inhales budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 µg two puffs twice daily, uses tiotropium 18 µg every morning to curb exertional symptoms when climbing control-tower stairwells, and empties one salbutamol metered-dose inhaler roughly every two months, typically before pick-up basketball games; he has never required mechanical ventilation, systemic corticosteroids in the past three years, or supplemental oxygen, and his last arterial saturation in the emergency department was 97 % on ambient air after a viral-triggered flare. Four years ago symmetric pain and swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints prompted evaluation by rheumatology; serology showed a rheumatoid factor of 112 IU/mL and anti-CCP antibody >300 U/mL, and plain films demonstrated juxta-articular osteopenia without erosions. He began methotrexate 20 mg orally once weekly with folic acid, later adding adalimumab 40 mg every other week when morning stiffness persisted beyond an hour. Over the last year Disease Activity Score-28 assessments have ranged 2.4–2.8, and he reports that joint discomfort now amounts to occasional stiffness after long flights that resolves with brief stretching; he has never developed pleuritis, pericarditis, vasculitic ulcers, scleritis, or cervical instability, and has no limitation in performing aircraft walk-arounds or lugging 15-kg test equipment. There is no history of crushing chest pressure, emergency catheterization, troponin elevation, paroxysmal dyspnea, orthopnea, pedal edema, or exertional diaphoresis suggestive of pump dysfunction. He jogs three kilometers twice weekly at a 5-minute pace without calf pain, rest discomfort, or color changes in his toes, and pedal pulses were documented as brisk at his last occupational fitness exam. Neurologic review is silent for transient speech disturbance, facial droop, monocular blindness, focal weakness, or imbalance, and he easily performs rapid mental calculations when auditing fuel-load spreadsheets. He denies memory lapses, personality change, or difficulty following complex flight-deck schematics. He completed childhood immunizations, has tested negative for HIV on three aviation medical certificates, consumes two craft beers on Friday nights, has never smoked cigarettes or vaped, and does not use illicit substances. His father, age 64, has seasonal allergies but no heart or vascular disease; his mother, age 61, has hypothyroidism. The patient’s weight has remained stable for five years. One year ago an insurance screening laboratory panel revealed a fasting plasma glucose of 108 mg/dL and glycated hemoglobin 5.9 %, for which he adopted a lower-carbohydrate meal plan and has since maintained fasting readings between 95 and 112 mg/dL on home glucometer checks; he takes no antihyperglycemic medications and has never experienced polyuria, blurred vision, neuropathic tingling, or foot ulceration. Current medications include methotrexate, adalimumab, budesonide-formoterol, tiotropium, albuterol as needed, folic acid 1 mg daily, and a daily multivitamin; he carries an epinephrine auto-injector because of an isolated childhood walnut anaphylaxis but has not used it in over fifteen years. Review of systems today is negative for dyspepsia, hematemesis, melena, jaundice, bruising, flank pain, hematuria, night sweats, unintended weight change, or fevers. On examination he appears fit, sits comfortably, and converses in full sentences. Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 118/68 mm Hg right arm seated, heart rate 74 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air, body-mass index 24 kg/m². Conjunctivae and sclerae are clear; oral mucosa is moist without ulcers. Carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit; jugular venous pulsation measures 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°. The point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp, with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Chest percussion is resonant; auscultation reveals slightly prolonged expiratory phase with scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender; liver span per percussion is 8 cm, edge is smooth, spleen is not palpable, and there is no ascites. Hands display minimal swelling at the second MCPs with full fist closure and no nodules; grip strength is symmetric. Skin shows a faint, well-healed psoriasiform plaque on the left elbow but no vasculitic lesions or digital ulcers. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric, with capillary refill under two seconds; there is no cyanosis or edema. Neurologic testing reveals fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, normal sensation, and a steady tandem gait. Laboratory studies drawn this morning demonstrate sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 115 mL/min/1.73 m²), fasting glucose 102 mg/dL, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 73 U/L, albumin 4.6 g/dL, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, white-blood-cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 282 × 10⁹/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 14 mm/h, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A 12-lead electrocardiogram records normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats/min with normal intervals and no pathologic Q waves or ST-segment deviation. Post-bronchodilator spirometry performed in clinic duplicates the external results, and a standing posteroanterior chest radiograph shows clear lung fields, mild hyperinflation, and a normal cardiac silhouette. The patient seeks assurance that his airway regimen is appropriate for the high-humidity environments he will encounter, clarification on safe storage of biologic injections while abroad, and a letter summarizing his current functional capacity for the airline medical desk.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums age points and weights for qualifying chronic diseases present at intake.
- Age 32: under 50 → 0 points.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: persistent asthma with airflow obstruction requiring daily inhaled therapy → +1.
- Rheumatic disease: established seropositive rheumatoid arthritis → +1, even though symptoms are controlled.
- Diabetes: HbA1c 5.9% and fasting glucose 102 mg/dL indicate prediabetes, not diabetes → 0.
- No other qualifying condition is documented → 0.
Total = 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
